extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on interference practice and the legal standards for establishing conception, reduction to practice, suppression/concealment, and priority of invention under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) (and related statutes/regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference practice basis (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 is the basis of interference practice for determining priority of invention between two parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference is an inter partes proceeding directed at determining the first to invent among parties, involving two or more pending applications naming different inventors or one or more pending applications and one or more unexpired patents naming different inventors; see 35 U.S.C. 135, 37 CFR Part 41, Subparts D and E and MPEP Chapter 2300. (Editor note: limited applicability for applications subject to AIA first‑inventor‑to‑file rules.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference parties and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference involves parties asserting inventorship/priority where claims are to the 'same patentable invention' or otherwise overlap in a count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter that is the basis of an interference is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) upon conclusion of an interference (unless acts showing prior invention were not in this country). Interference practice operates to the exclusion of ex parte practice under 37 CFR 1.131 when claims are to the same patentable invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority awarded based on conception, reduction to practice, and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority may be awarded to a party who conceived before another and either (a) constructively reduced to practice earlier, (b) actually reduced to practice earlier, or (c) conceived earlier and coupled later reduction to practice with reasonable diligence from a time just prior to the other party's conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority scenarios are illustrated with time charts (C = conception; R = reduction to practice; Ra = actual; Rc = constructive; TD = commencement of diligence). Diligence from TD to reduction times can establish priority; absence of abandonment/suppression/concealment is required in many scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.131 does not apply in interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference practice operates to the exclusion of ex parte practice under 37 CFR 1.131.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.131 permits showing an actual date of invention to antedate references, but where an application claim is to the same patentable invention claimed in a domestic patent it requires an interference rather than an affidavit under 1.131. Subject matter in an interference is not open to further inquiry under 1.131 during the interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost counts in an interference are not per se statutory prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of an interference count alone does not make its subject matter statutory prior art to the losing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost count subject matter that is available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 may be used alone or in combination under 35 U.S.C. 103. But res judicata/collateral estoppel principles (e.g., In re Deckler) may bar claims patentably indistinguishable from the lost count even if the lost count is not statutory prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Made in this country" requirement (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g)/104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is limited to an invention that is 'made' in this country; acts of conception, reduction to practice and diligence must be demonstrated in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions per amended pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 allow establishment of invention dates in NAFTA/WTO member countries after specified dates (e.g., NAFTA member country on or after Dec. 8, 1993; WTO non‑NAFTA on or after Jan. 1, 1996). Foreign reduction to practice with knowledge brought into U.S. may be only evidence of conception (Colbert v. Lofdahl).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression, concealment, and abandonment doctrine (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention though completed is deemed abandoned, suppressed, or concealed if, within a reasonable time after completion, no steps are taken to make the invention publicly known (e.g., failure to file, publish, or publicly use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider delay to file, public disclosure, and use in determining suppression/concealment; whether delay is 'mere' or creates an inference of suppression is case‑by‑case. Suppression/concealment doctrines can alter priority by treating a de facto first inventor who suppressed/ concealed as a later inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of suppression or concealment from delay in filing
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference proceeding, a delay between actual reduction to practice and filing may give rise to an inference of suppression or concealment that can prevent relying on the earlier actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length of delay is evaluated case‑by‑case; 'mere delay, without more, is not sufficient' but excessive unexplained delay can create the inference (examples: 4 years prima facie unreasonably long; 3 months potentially excusable depending on circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression or concealment need not be attributed to the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay or suppression that gives rise to an inference does not have to be the act of the inventor personally; it may be attributable to assignee/employer/others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show employer or attorney workload/delay may still lead to an inference; attribution is not required for the doctrine to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of suppression or concealment is rebuttable
rubrics_metrics.description: An inference of suppression or concealment can be rebutted by evidence such as renewed activity just prior to the other party’s entry into the field together with diligent filing of an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that can rebut includes activity directed to perfecting the invention, preparing the application, or preparing other compounds within the scope; evidence of commercialization alone may be insufficient to rebut. Case citations: Lutzker v. Plet; Holmwood v. Cherpeck; Engelhardt v. Judd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment distinct from suppression/concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of suppression or concealment may not amount to a finding of abandonment; an invention cannot be abandoned until it is first reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases emphasize that abandonment (loss of right to patent) is a different legal outcome from suppression/concealment in priority analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception — definition and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is 'the complete performance of the mental part of the inventive act' — the formation in the mind of the inventor of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention as it is to be applied in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception is established when the invention is made sufficiently clear to enable one skilled in the art to reduce it to practice without extensive experimentation or inventive skill; every limitation of the count must have been known to the inventor at the time of alleged conception and conception must be proved by corroborating evidence. Case examples: Townsend v. Smith; Hiatt v. Ziegler; Coleman v. Dines; Hybritech; Hitzeman v. Rutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception must be in the mind of the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must form a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operable invention; noninventor testimony as to inventor's meaning is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony by a noninventor about an inventor's notebook or meaning may be insufficient to establish what the inventors actually conceived (Bosies v. Benedict).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception requires contemporaneous recognition and appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be contemporaneous recognition and appreciation of the invention for conception to be established; accidental and unappreciated duplication does not establish conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor need not know the invention will work or its patentability, but must have recognized the invention's features contemporaneously. Conception of a species does not necessarily equal conception of the genus or other species; for complex biochemical/genetic matters, detailed constitution and method to obtain it may be required (Amgen, Fiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of others' ideas allowed if inventor maintains intellectual domination
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may adopt ideas, suggestions, and materials from employees, consultants, or others provided the inventor maintains intellectual domination over making the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted material that proves key to the invention does not defeat conception so long as the inventor maintains intellectual domination (Morse v. Porter; Staehelin v. Secher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Previously abandoned application not copending is evidence only of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandoned application with which no subsequent application was copending serves only as evidence of conception, not as a constructive reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing of an original application that was later abandoned abandons the benefit of that filing as a constructive reduction to practice unless requirements (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 120) are satisfied for benefit claim. (In re Costello.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice (actual vs constructive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice may be actual (physical embodiment tested to work) or constructive (occurs when a patent application on the claimed invention is filed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an application serves as conception and constructive reduction to practice of subject matter described therein; inventor relying on a filed application need not provide separate evidence of conception or actual reduction to practice for that subject matter (Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction to practice requires compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre‑AIA 112 and 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking benefit of an earlier‑filed U.S. patent application, the earlier application must meet requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) for the subject matter of the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The earlier application must meet enablement and written description requirements, include all limitations of the interference count or show the absent text is necessarily comprehended, and provide sufficient 'how to make' and 'how to use' disclosure. The written description must be sufficient so that the necessary and only reasonable construction by a person skilled in the art clearly supports each positive limitation in the count (Hyatt v. Boone; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Edwards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice — two‑prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish an actual reduction to practice in an interference, a party must (1) have constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met every element of the interference count, and (2) show the embodiment or process operated for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual reduction to practice requires a physical or tangible form showing every element; demonstration of workability via sufficient testing is necessary though not necessarily commercial success. The sufficiency and character of testing varies with invention complexity. (Eaton v. Evans; Wetmore v. Quick; Scott v. Finney.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing required to establish actual reduction to practice depends on the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and extent of testing required to demonstrate reduction to practice depends on the particular facts and nature of the invention; tests must demonstrate that the invention will work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests conducted under laboratory conditions must either duplicate actual use conditions or establish a relationship between test conditions and intended functional setting; less than all actual use conditions may suffice where appropriate. For processes producing products, demonstration that the product made is satisfactory may be required (Gellert v. Wanberg; Wells v. Fremont; Birmingham v. Randall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and appreciation required for reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice requires contemporaneous appreciation of the invention by the inventor; subsequent recognition or later testing cannot be used to show that contemporaneous appreciation existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of later testing may be admitted only to show that an embodiment was produced that met the limitations of the count, not to establish contemporaneous appreciation. Cases: Cooper v. Goldfarb; Meitzner v. Corte; Estee Lauder v. L'Oreal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship/derivation and 35 U.S.C. 101/102(f) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 requires that whoever invents or discovers the claimed invention must be named as the inventor(s) for a patent to be granted; derivation from another can support a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation addresses originality (who invented the subject matter), while priority focuses on who invented first; where derivation can be shown, a 102(f) rejection is proper. (Ex parte Kusko; Price v. Symsek.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology used in priority analysis (C, R, Ra, Rc, TD)
rubrics_metrics.description: In priority time charts: C = conception; R = reduction to practice (actual or constructive); Ra = actual reduction to practice; Rc = constructive reduction to practice; TD = commencement of diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These symbols are used to illustrate priority scenarios and to analyze who is awarded priority under various combinations of conception, reduction, and diligence.
